sections.h: How Luke reworks Mark in Luke 9
sections.b: Luke 9 shows Luke's method with Mark clearly. He follows Mark 6 through the feeding of the five thousand, then leaves out Mark 6:45–8:26 (the "great omission") and resumes at Peter's confession. He corrects Mark's "King Herod" to "tetrarch" (Luke 9:7), replaces Hebrew and Aramaic words with Greek ones ("Master" for "Rabbi," "truly" for "Amen"), adds Jesus' prayer at turning points (Luke 9:18; 9:28–29), and adds details of his own, such as the cross carried "every day" (Luke 9:23) and the conversation about Jesus' "exodus" (Luke 9:31). Henry Cadbury showed how consistently Luke improves Mark's Greek. Then, at Luke 9:51, he leaves Mark for ten chapters and builds the journey to Jerusalem from sayings shared with Matthew and from his own material.

sections.h: The Twelve sent out in Luke
sections.b: Luke's Jesus gives the Twelve "power and authority" over demons and diseases and sends them to announce the kingdom and heal, carrying nothing (Luke 9:1–6). They return and report, and Luke calls them "apostles," those sent (Luke 9:10). A second, larger sending of seventy-two follows (Luke 10:1–20), found only in Luke. The two missions model the church's mission in Acts, where the same pairing of word and healing continues. Jesus' saying "Whoever hears you hears me" (Luke 10:16) rests on the Jewish principle that an agent stands for the one who sent him (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5); the churches differ on how far it reaches beyond the first messengers.

common: The mission of the Twelve in Luke 9 is a model for the church's mission in Acts.
uncommon: Luke's two missions (9:1 and 10:1) come from two sources, Mark and Q, rather than two historical sendings.

sections.h: Herod Antipas wonders who Jesus is
sections.b: Luke gives Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, a thread of his own. Having beheaded John, he hears of Jesus' work and is at a loss: some say John has been raised, others Elijah or one of the ancient prophets. "So who is this man?" he asks, and keeps looking for a chance to see him (Luke 9:7–9). Luke does not tell the story of John's death (compare Mark 6:17–29), but the wish to see Jesus returns when Pilate sends Jesus to Herod at the trial (Luke 23:6–12). Josephus says Herod killed John at Machaerus, fearing his influence on the crowds.

In Luke, Peter's confession is "God's Messiah" (Luke 9:20), the anointed one God has chosen, a phrase Luke repeats at the cross (Luke 23:35) and that echoes "the Lord's Messiah" of Simeon (Luke 2:26) and Psalm 2:2. Jesus at once orders silence and explains that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised (Luke 9:21–22). In Luke's account there is no blessing of Peter and no rebuke of Jesus by Peter; the confession leads straight to the cross.
sections.refs: Luke 9:18–22; Luke 2:26; Luke 23:35; Psalm 2:2; Acts 4:26; Matthew 16:13–23; Mark 8:27–33

sections.h: The Son of Man must suffer (Luke 9)
sections.b: Luke 9 contains two of Jesus' predictions of his death. In the first, the Son of Man "has to" suffer, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed and be raised (Luke 9:22); in the second, he is about to be "handed over into human hands" (Luke 9:44), a phrase that plays in Aramaic on "son of man" and "sons of men." The Son of Man who has nowhere to rest his head (Luke 9:58) will come in his own glory, his Father's and the angels' (Luke 9:26).

sections.h: The cost of following in Luke 9
sections.b: Luke places the hardest sayings about following Jesus at the start of the journey to Jerusalem. Anyone who wants to come behind him must say no to himself and pick up his cross "every day" (Luke 9:23), a phrase only Luke has. Three would-be followers meet him on the road: one learns that the Son of Man has no home, one that the call outranks even burying his father, one that a plowman who looks back is no use to the kingdom (Luke 9:57–62). The third request echoes Elisha's (1 Kings 19:19–21); Jesus asks more than Elijah did. Scholars debate whether these demands were for every disciple or for those who left everything to travel with Jesus.

common: Following Jesus means putting him before family, home and safety.
uncommon: The radical sayings were meant for traveling missionaries, not for settled believers (Theissen).

sections.b: Luke tells the scene while Jesus is praying (Luke 9:28–29). He avoids the word "transformed" and speaks of Jesus' face, recalling Moses' shining face (Exodus 34:29). Only Luke says what Moses and Elijah talked about: Jesus' "exodus," which he would complete in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Only Luke says the disciples were heavy with sleep (Luke 9:32), and the voice calls Jesus "the Chosen One" (Luke 9:35), the title of Isaiah's servant (Isaiah 42:1). Luke dates it "some eight days" after the confession, where Mark and Matthew say six.
sections.refs: Luke 9:28–36; Exodus 34:29–35; Isaiah 42:1; Deuteronomy 18:15; Mark 9:2–8; Matthew 17:1–8

sections.b: On the mountain Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his exodos, which he was going to complete in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The word means departure and death, but with Moses present it also recalls the exodus from Egypt. Many scholars read Luke's journey section (Luke 9:51–19:44) as a new exodus, with Jesus as the prophet like Moses leading God's people through his death, resurrection and ascension; David Moessner traced parallels with Moses' journey in Deuteronomy.
sections.refs: Luke 9:31; Luke 9:51; Exodus 12:41; Deuteronomy 18:15; Isaiah 43:16–19; 2 Peter 1:15

sections.b: The voice from the cloud in Luke 9:35 ends with "Listen to him!", the words Moses used of the prophet God would raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15). With Moses standing there, God points to Jesus as that prophet. Luke makes the link explicit in Acts, where Peter and Stephen quote Deuteronomy 18:15 about Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37).

Luke opens the journey to Jerusalem with "the days ... before he would be taken up" (Luke 9:51). The noun analēmpsis is related to the verb Luke uses for the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22) and that the Greek Old Testament uses for Elijah taken up in the windstorm (2 Kings 2:9–11). From its first step the road to the cross is also the road to the Father. The "two men" of the transfiguration (Luke 9:30) return at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4) and the ascension (Acts 1:10).
sections.refs: Luke 9:30–31; Luke 9:51; Luke 24:4; Luke 24:51; Acts 1:2; Acts 1:9–11; 2 Kings 2:9–11

sections.b: Luke 9 is full of Elijah. People say Jesus is Elijah come back (Luke 9:8, 19); Elijah appears with Moses on the mountain (Luke 9:30); Jesus will be "taken up" as Elijah was (Luke 9:51; 2 Kings 2:9–11). But when James and John want to call fire down on a Samaritan village, as Elijah did to the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10–12), Jesus rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55). And when a would-be follower asks to say goodbye at home, as Elisha asked Elijah, Jesus refuses what Elijah allowed (Luke 9:61–62; 1 Kings 19:19–21). Luke presents Jesus as greater than Elijah and different from him.

At the start of the journey a Samaritan village refuses Jesus because he is going to Jerusalem, the rival of their holy mountain, Gerizim (Luke 9:52–53). James and John want fire from heaven; Jesus rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55). Almost at once Jesus tells a story in which a Samaritan is the one who shows mercy to a wounded man that a priest and a Levite passed by (Luke 10:30–37), echoing the Samaritans who once cared for captives from Judah and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:15). In Acts, Samaria receives the word, and John, who had wanted fire, prays for the Samaritans to receive the Spirit (Acts 8:14–17). Josephus records real violence between Samaritans and Jews in this period (Antiquities 18.29–30; 20.118–136).
sections.refs: Luke 9:51–56; Luke 10:25–37; Luke 17:11–19; 2 Chronicles 28:8–15; John 4:9; John 4:20; Acts 8:4–25

common: The good Samaritan shows that love of neighbor crosses every ethnic and religious border.
uncommon: The parable is shaped on 2 Chronicles 28:8–15, where Samaritans rescue Judean captives and bring them to Jericho (Spencer).

sections.b: When a Samaritan village refuses Jesus, James and John offer to call down fire to consume it, as Elijah did (2 Kings 1:10–12). Jesus turns and rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55). Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add his words "You do not know what spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them." Though probably not part of what Luke wrote, those words became one of the most quoted texts against religious violence, and the scene itself shows Jesus refusing to meet rejection with force.

Luke's Jesus sends out seventy-two messengers (some manuscripts say seventy). The Hebrew text of Genesis 10 lists seventy nations, the Greek Septuagint seventy-two, so many readers see in the number a sign of the coming mission to all nations, after the Twelve, who stand for Israel's tribes. Others link it to Moses' seventy elders (Numbers 11:16–26) or to the seventy-two translators of the Letter of Aristeas.

sections.h: "I was watching Satan fall like lightning" (Luke 10:18)
sections.b: When the seventy-two report that even demons obey them, Jesus says he was watching Satan fall like lightning out of heaven (Luke 10:18). Readers have placed the fall before creation (with Isaiah 14:12, the "Lucifer" passage), at Jesus' testing, in the mission itself, or at the end (Revelation 12:7–10). Susan Garrett argues that Luke-Acts tells the story of Satan's overthrow, which begins here. Jesus gives his messengers authority over "every power the enemy has" (Luke 10:19) but tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven.

common: Luke 10:18 describes Satan's fall from heaven before the creation of humans.
uncommon: The saying describes Satan's defeat taking place in the exorcisms of Jesus' messengers (Garrett, many modern scholars).

sections.b: Jesus tells the seventy-two not to rejoice that spirits obey them but that their names "stand written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). The image goes back to Moses' plea to be wiped out of God's book (Exodus 32:32) and the "scroll of life" of Psalm 69:28, and forward to the book of life in Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 20:12.
sections.refs: Luke 10:20; Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 20:12

sections.h: The lawyer, the neighbor and the Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37)
sections.b: In Luke a lawyer, not Jesus, joins the love of God (Deuteronomy 6:5) and the love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) as the answer to "What should I do to inherit eternal life?", and Jesus approves (Luke 10:25–28). Jewish texts of the period already joined the two (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Philo). The new step is the parable: asked "who is my neighbor?", Jesus tells of a Samaritan who rescues a wounded man and asks who "became a neighbor" (Luke 10:36). The question moves from whom I must love to whom I can become a neighbor to, and Leviticus 19:34 had already extended love to the foreigner.
sections.refs: Luke 10:25–37; Leviticus 19:18; Leviticus 19:34; Deuteronomy 6:5; Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 22:34–40

common: "Neighbor" means anyone in need, whatever their people or religion.

sections.b: Hospitality runs through Luke 9–10. Jesus welcomes the crowd and feeds it (Luke 9:11–17). A Samaritan village refuses him lodging (Luke 9:53). His messengers go out with nothing, depending on houses that receive them, and are told to stay in one house and eat what is set before them (Luke 9:4; 10:5–8). In the parable a Samaritan pays an innkeeper to care for a stranger (Luke 10:34–35), and Martha takes Jesus into her home as her guest (Luke 10:38). Early Christian missionaries depended on the same welcome; the Didache warns against those who abuse it.

Luke tells one scene of the sisters, without naming their village or their brother: Martha welcomes Jesus and is busy with serving, while Mary sits at his feet listening; Jesus tells the worried Martha that one thing is needed and that Mary has chosen the good share (Luke 10:38–42). John's Gospel shows the same characters at Bethany: Martha active and outspoken, Mary at Jesus' feet (John 11:20–32; John 12:1–3). The scene became the church's classic picture of the active and contemplative lives.

sections.h: Mary at Jesus' feet, Martha's service (Luke 10:38–42)
sections.b: Mary sits at Jesus' feet, the posture of a disciple learning from a teacher (compare Acts 22:3), and Jesus says her choice will not be taken from her (Luke 10:39, 42). Many read this as Jesus accepting a woman as a disciple. Martha's work is called diakonia (Luke 10:40), the word later used for ministry and for deacons (Acts 6:1–4; Romans 16:1). Interpreters differ on what Luke intends: some see support for women as learners and teachers; Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza argues that Luke prefers the silent listener to the active minister; others note that Jesus faults Martha's anxiety, not her service.

The Twelve are sent to "announce the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:2) and the seventy-two to say "The kingdom of God has drawn near to you" (Luke 10:9), even to towns that refuse them (Luke 10:11). Jesus promises that some standing with him will "see the kingdom of God" before they die (Luke 9:27), a saying read of the transfiguration, of Easter and Pentecost, of AD 70, or of the kingdom present in his works. A plowman who looks back is not suited to it (Luke 9:62).
sections.refs: Luke 9:2; Luke 9:11; Luke 9:27; Luke 9:60–62; Luke 10:9–11; Acts 28:31

sections.b: Luke puts Jesus at prayer before Peter's confession (Luke 9:18) and on the mountain, where his face changes "while he was praying" (Luke 9:28–29); Mark and Matthew have neither. In Luke 10:21 Jesus, rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, thanks the Father for revealing his work to little children. Mary, sitting at his feet to hear his word (Luke 10:39–42), became for many Christians the picture of contemplative prayer; the churches differ on whether that makes contemplation a higher calling.

Asked who became a neighbor, the lawyer answers, "The one who acted with mercy toward him" (Luke 10:37). The phrase "to do mercy with" someone is the Greek Bible's way of saying "to do hesed," loyal love (Genesis 24:12; Ruth 1:8). The Samaritan's heart goes out to the man (Luke 10:33), the word Luke uses for Jesus at Nain (Luke 7:13) and for the father of the lost son (Luke 15:20). Jesus' command is to do the same.
sections.refs: Luke 10:33–37; Luke 7:13; Luke 15:20; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:8; Matthew 9:13

sections.b: Told to a lawyer who asked "who is my neighbor?", the parable of the man on the Jericho road is found only in Luke. A priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan, the hearers' enemy, stops, binds his wounds, takes him to an inn and pays for his care. Jesus then asks which of the three became a neighbor. The church fathers read it as an allegory of Christ rescuing fallen humanity (Origen, Augustine); modern interpreters mostly read it as an answer to the lawyer, and Amy-Jill Levine stresses the shock of a Samaritan hero to Jewish hearers, warning against readings that make the priest and Levite stand for a heartless Judaism.

Jesus "fixed his face firmly on going to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), which opens the long journey of Luke 9:51–19:44. The idiom echoes the Servant who made his face hard as flint (Isaiah 50:7) and the prophet told to set his face toward Jerusalem (Ezekiel 21:2). For Luke, Jerusalem is the city where prophets die (Luke 13:33–34) and where Jesus will complete his exodus (Luke 9:31), and it is also where the church begins (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8).
